segments.description: Hi, Coaches, and welcome to the 2022 Virtual Grand Slam Coaches Conference. I'm thrilled to be here today with two powerful women coaches who are change makers in the game in Australia and abroad, and they are Sarah Stone and Beresa Kolowski. A little bit about Sarah first. Sarah is the founder and CEO of the WTCA. She's had some really successful relationships with WTA and collegiate athletes, and she's very well known for her technical development, as well as her leadership, particularly in women's tennis. No one to Betty who's just rushed in from the Australian Open, watching a player on court. As a high-performance tennis Australia coach, she has extensive experience from the UK to Europe through to Australia working for federations and in the private sector, and she's the current coach of Jamie Fowler. So welcome so much, Sarah and Betty, and thanks so much for being here. Hi, Karen. Thanks for having us. Thanks for having us. It's our pleasure to have you, and thank you for sharing your knowledge and some information that we found really useful on their on-demand session that most coaches have either watched yesterday when it first became available or can watch ongoing. The four components that I really found important were your main headings, teamwork, know your player, working together and leadership. And I'll probably just ask Sarah first. This seems like a Sarah question. How

do you come up with the topic, creating culture and collaborative coaching? Well, we came up with that because Betty and I have joined forces recently to start in Academy of Melbourne. We'd be best friends forever, but it's totally different when you start to work with a player, and you have to really be on the same page because there's times that we're not on the same court. There were new players that I was working with that Betty had previously coached, and we needed to really spend time figuring out how we were going to approach it. Betty's been with them for a long time. I wanted to make sure I use the same language, and when you're working with another coach, it's particularly important to be supportive. Sometimes you might not have the exact same idea as them, and in your own head you might think, well, I know better about that, but that's something you want to make sure that you just keep it in your own head. You support each other when you're working with a player, and that's what we've spent a lot of time doing over the last six, seven, eight months, and it's been really successful because we have really good communication, and we're honest with each other about where we think each other's right and where we might not be, but we always do that away from the player that's never in front of the player, and we always support each other with our language to the player. Yeah, it's super essential to be able to communicate. That's great. When you think

making changes, because they know where they are, and they're happy where they are, but sometimes to make a small adjustment might mean rather than be 50 in the world, they're 15 in the world, and that can be pretty scary, because they're pretty comfortable being 50 in the world, they know how much money they're making, and they could risk it because if it goes wrong, they might be outside top 100, so when change is such a difficult thing for everybody, we get into routines, trust and trust in your coach, and trust in their ability to make that change with you is something, it's pretty important, and your whole career is kind of, it's not exactly in their hands of a coach, but they play a major part in developing what you're doing, your results, and things like that, so keeping your words, sticking to what you say, being honest, representing the player well when you speak about them anywhere, anytime to any other player, or any other coach, I think these sorts of things build trust, and keeping what they say confidential, I think that's a big part of a coaching relationship, you might think I'll just say this to that person, and just pass that on, and no one's, you don't say anything, and I won't, and then all of a sudden that person says don't say anything, and it spreads everywhere, so that trust and belief, and sometimes they share some things with you that are tricky, especially young players,

it really comes down to, for me, is how you relay the message to the player, and understanding who you're working with, and I think that's something that I've tried to work on over the last few years, is really, sometimes, you know, it's not about us, it's not about us, the coaches, it's really about them, and it's trying to find out, you know, the best way to communicate with your players, and I think that's what I seem to pick up a lot from some of the best coaches in the world, is how simplistic they go about their day-to-day business with players, and coaches, and communication, and that for me has been really the forefront of everything I'm trying to do at the moment. Yeah, nice one. Yeah, mine's actually about Tennis, is my dad from a technical standpoint, he's a very good coach, he's coached for a very long time, since I was about three years old, he was coaching a player, Barbara Potter, who at that time was number seven in the world, so I was lucky to have a parent that knew a lot about that, and was very good technically. Outside of that, obviously, lots of people around, Kathy Rinaldi, I love talking to Tennis also with Prati, she's great. I would say most people, for me, mentor-wise, is the people that have influenced me in my life to understand myself the best, and so that I can be the best version of myself when I'm with my athletes, so very good friends of myself and Betty, and also

Sam Stoza, you know, a lot of players stayed there, Julian and Marilyn Kahn, they're from, well, they're from England, but now in Australia, they were just people that took a lot of time with me and let me be myself and help me understand myself fully, and I think that when you get that, you're able to present yourself and communicate well with the players and know what you stand for and things like that, so some of my biggest influences have not actually been Tennis people, they've just been people that have been supportive as me as an individual. Yeah, really invested in you to be unique, they're wonderful answers, and I like that they're not just Tennis, and that it's a very well-rounded involvement from a range of people, so thank you for sharing, and for the coaches who are listening in, they might look for mentors that are inside Tennis and also outside of Tennis as well. The switching is a little bit, we have a question, and I know both of you are working particularly interested in the development in the female space, but there is a significant dropout of girls, female players, in Australia, and from that 14- year-old age group, and have you got any tips on how we can keep these girls in our sport? So, Stonie, you want me to take this one? Yeah, go for it, you have a crack, it's a good question, I'm interested in your answer. Well, I love the fact that you're sharing, thank you.

No, look, I think exactly right, you know, there is a big dropout of this age group and it's tough, I think again, it comes down to caring, it comes down to understanding that every player is going through their own journey, and quite often with this age group, they're comparing themselves to other girls in their age group that are probably doing a little better than them, and what we really need to understand is not only people, but coaches, is that everyone is on their own path, there is a reason why we're on this path, and it's trying to figure out how we can get them a little better, you know, one day at a time, and understand what they want from the sport, because not every kid that's walking through the gate, you know, is wanting to be a professional tennis player, some of them have a different reason for attending, you know, we have a couple of kids that just love being around the other kids in the squads, and that's enough to keep them coming, and I think that's important to understand what they're, what they're coming for, and also our job is to make sure that they're whilst they're coming in, that they're not only part of a positive environment, but they're actually, we're improving every, you know, aspect as we can from them on the court and off the court, but we have to understand that, I think clearly is why are they playing tennis, what do they want out of it right now, what they

want out of it right now may not be the same in 12 months time, so we need to keep understanding and respecting where they're at, and keep communicating this, and I quite often ask players to, you know, what is your process goal, what do you want to achieve out of today, and making sure that that's the only thing that we're worried about, we're not worried about what everyone else is doing, so that's been partly my experience with this age group, Cathy. And asking a lot of questions, I can sense there, Betty, it's something that, you know, you review constantly asking the player, what's driving you, what's motivating you, what are your goals, where are you at, even though you're a high performance coach, I can imagine that you'd still be happy to coach the younger, less experienced players, and just for the joy of playing tennis. Yeah, absolutely, and look, at the end of the day, as much as high performance is a wonderful space, really, we've got to take care of what's happening below, because, you know, that is actually important, that's what's pushing forwards, and we need to take care of that age group, especially in the female age groups, you know, we need to make sure that they're part of groups where they're, maybe the focus sometimes is a little bit too much, it's sometimes too intense to be the only sole focus, you're the best player in the squad, and everything's about you, and I think it's important for them to learn

how to be around other players, that it's not always about them, and that it's also just partly them turning up to a great environment where they look forward to it, and, you know, the last thing, they come off the court going, I can't wait to be there tomorrow or the following day, I mean, how good is that? That is amazing, yeah, I have to chime in, I'm not going to let this question slide through, there's two keys for me, one is coaches need to be aware of clicks, at these age groups, girls tend to get into little clicks, and you might, you've got to be aware that you might see one that's on the outside, and they almost get ostracised, it's just, it's something that's socially, you know, you need to be aware that that happens, and just make sure that there's inclusion there, because if that one gets left out, and then they even start, sometimes we've heard of things where there's little WhatsApp groups, where they're all against some other, one of the girls, well that girl's not going to play the sport, so coaches need to be aware of these things, the second thing is the significant amount of social pressure on women to look a certain way, that starts girls start to look at their bodies, and they're changing, and for girls to actually start their period, they need to have 17% body fat, coaches need to be aware of this girls aren't just going a little bit like thicker with their body fat, because they're not eating

right, and boys go lean, the testosterone, they go lean, girls go, and so male coaches sometimes don't understand, particularly male coaches, that girls need that to actually, it's biological, so they might say, oh well, you know, you just need to get a bit fitter, you're a little bit, you know, you're looking a bit thick, or we need to this, that need to be super careful of those comments, and these changes start with 11, 12, and that is a huge thing that drives girls away from the game, because of the social pressure of the way girls should look, it's already on top of them, and then you're not looking at that biological part of life, so they're the two things that I think that coaches need to be really aware of. Can I just cut, sorry, can I just cut in again, is one of, one of the things that I think Stoney knew would agree with this, and you know, we've probably seen some of this happen in the past, is just even punishments, how we use the word punishments or consequences, you know, you see players are missing, especially again with young females, it really depends on the personality, but I would imagine this can work in both genders, especially is, you know, I've seen this happen where players are missing a serve, they're really trying to work on something, but they keep missing in the net, and the coaches like, okay, do some push-ups, because you know, you miss two in a row, or whatever it is, I think using consequences in

that way is something that we're not really not fans of, because we've never seen it actually work very well, and I look, everyone has their own coaching philosophy, but I know Sarah and I really agree, we don't like that, we don't actually even impose that for a second. Accountability, yes, punishments, because someone's trying to hit a serve in, definitely no, from our end, so I just yeah, I thought I'd just speak about that, because it was something fresh in my mind that I thought was worth obviously talking about. Yeah, that's great, and some varied responses there, and they all contribute to the enjoyment of the sport, which is really what it comes down to, the joy part of enjoyment, and keeping those skills and boys playing the sport, and then, you know, as generations go on, they'll bring their own children, hopefully some daughters as well, into tennis, and love the game. So that was an excellent question, and some really great answers there, and really not that hard to try and implement some of the learnings that you've just given us, either, then they're not insurmountable. You mentioned Betty, coaching philosophy, and Sarah, you mentioned culture, and I'm going to try and ask you a question that intertwines these two, with Champion Academy, which you're both representing as business owners, and I can imagine you both have your own coaching philosophies, how does that also impact the culture that you bring? how about Sarah, coaching philosophy into the culture? They're distinct, they're actually, they're distinctly different and almost the same, it's funny with us, we go about the way we do it a little bit differently, we look for the same checkpoints probably technically, so not so much as not from a stylistic, we're not into style, like every forehand should go here versus there, or every serve should be a pinpoint versus a platform, it's whatever's best for the athlete, but where are they making contact with the ball, where is their positioning, how's their positioning, those things are things that we both agree with very clearly, Betty loves the analytics, there's certain things that, and I go about coaching a little bit more like someone's throwing paint under canvas, but it's the way we allow each other to be ourselves, and we know exactly where each other's strengths and weaknesses are, and we support both sides, and I think that's sort of the way our philosophy, the philosophy is more about our athlete-centred, like the person first, that is one thing that's very firm for both of us, and then we just kind of let each other go like that, and I think that that's, you know, I'm not huge about philosophy, I know some people are, I think it's a part of it, but I think just treating people well, and caring about them as a person first and foremost, and don't be so fixated on trying to make things look

how your own shots look, a lot of coaches teach their own shots because they like the technique, even if it's not good, that's okay, they teach it because that's what they know, like get outside of your box, and have asked the athlete who's their favourite player, who do they like to watch, what works for them, it's all about what works for the athlete over the coach in there, and sometimes Harry. Yeah. Athlete-centred would be a big part of your coaching philosophy, Betty? Absolutely, yeah absolutely, and I have a running joke because I probably speak to Sarah more than I speak to my partner during the day, I think we have about a million conversations because we're always discussing, you know, this is what happened, how can we get this player to see this, what's the vision, you know, we have a, we have a certain way how we go about our assessments of the player, you know, he's a lot of footage to backs things up, we discuss, yeah, we discuss every player honestly, a fair bit, we're very thorough with that, we talk about it, and if I can't be with the player then Sarah knows exactly what I've been doing, what it looks like, the player's very clear on what that vision is, so again it comes down to, look, it's tiring, but lucky I like Sarah, so I do speak to her a lot, and I think we have these enjoyable conversations, you know, we do go off topic sometimes, but we do discuss these on a very much regular basis. Well, I could imagine if our session went on for

Go ahead though. I think, I think inclusive, to be honest, I think inclusive, we don't like the, look, one thing I've probably learnt is, I'm not into whoever's got the best results, come on in and, you know, we'll throw your arms around you, we try and throw our arms around players that, you know, want the best thing for their tennis, and we're there really to support that dream as best as we can, so if I was to explain how the, how the culture looks, it's inclusive, we have standards, we hold players accountable, but at the same time, we're also human beings that care about people and we're all about, you know, we want what you want, so we want to be the people that can support that. The caring has certainly shone through today, absolutely.
